title: Mode of Address Standard
summary: How we address clients, leaders, and colleagues is part of our professionalism — every interaction should communicate respect, courtesy, professionalism, dignity, and order.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, how we address people is part of our professionalism.
Every therapist is expected to address clients, leaders and colleagues in a manner that communicates respect, courtesy, professionalism, dignity, and order.
The relationship may differ between a client, colleague and leader, but respect remains the standard in every interaction.
At Zura Spa, familiarity does not remove professionalism, friendship does not permit disrespect, and leadership does not permit anyone to belittle another person.
Our mode of address should help create an environment where everyone understands who is being referred to, the person's professional role, and the respect expected in the relationship.

sections.title: 1. Our Standard Mode of Address — Addressing Therapists
paragraphs: Therapists should normally be addressed by their work name preceded by "Therapist" or "Thr."
Examples: Therapist Jane, Thr. Jane, Therapist Clara, Thr. Olivia.

This applies when therapists are referring to one another professionally, particularly in front of clients, during handovers, during meetings, during training, in official communication, and when discussing work responsibilities.
The purpose is not excessive formality. It is to maintain a clear professional identity.

sections.title: 2. Addressing Therapists by Leadership Role
paragraphs: Where a therapist holds a recognized leadership responsibility, they may be addressed by the role.
Examples include Manager, Staff Manager (SM), Client Manager (CM), Supervisor (SP), Lead Therapist (LT), and Therapist Guide (TG).
Examples: "Please inform the SM." "The CM will attend to the client." "Please confirm with the SP." "The LT will assess the routine." "Please speak with the TG about the technique."
Where helpful, the role may also be combined with the person's work name: SM Jane, CM Clara, SP Olivia, LT Stacey, TG Mabel.
The objective is to make responsibilities and leadership relationships clear without creating an atmosphere of superiority or fear.

sections.title: 3. Addressing Clients Within the Team
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, everyone receiving our service is regarded as a client at all times, including when we are speaking about them internally.
In the same way that a hospital consistently refers to the person receiving care as a patient, we consistently recognize the person receiving our service as a client.
Therefore, when referring to a client within the team, use Client + Name.
Examples: Client Sam, Client John, Client Grace, Client Michael.
Examples: "Client Sam is waiting in Room 2." "Client John requested medium pressure." "Client Grace has completed her session." "Client Michael reported pain around his shoulder."
This is preferable to descriptions such as "That man," "That woman," "The guy inside," "That customer," "The person in Room 2," "That Indian man," "The tall man," or "The woman that came yesterday."
Where the client's name is known, use the client's name.

sections.title: 4. Asking for a Client's Name
paragraphs: Therapists should not avoid learning the client's name when the interaction requires it.
Where necessary, politely ask: "Please Sir/Ma, may I have your name?" or "May I know your name please?"
Once the name is known, use it appropriately.

The client's name helps personalize the interaction, reduce confusion, improve handovers, prevent therapists from identifying clients through physical descriptions, improve professionalism, and help clients feel recognized.

sections.title: 5. Addressing Clients Directly
paragraphs: When communicating directly with a client, therapists should use a respectful form of address appropriate to the situation.
Approved forms include: Mr. + Name, Ms. + Name, Sir, Ma, and Madam.
Examples: "Welcome, Mr. Samuel." "Are you comfortable, Ms. Grace?" "How is the pressure, Sir?" "Please turn over when you're ready, Ma." "Thank you, Madam."
Where the client's preferred title is known, that preference should be respected.

sections.title: 6. The Tone Is as Important as the Word
paragraphs: Calling someone "Sir," "Ma," or "Madam" does not automatically make communication respectful.
The same word can sound respectful or insulting depending on tone, facial expression, volume, body language, and context.
Example: "Yes, Sir." said calmly communicates respect. But "YES SIR!" said sarcastically, aggressively or dismissively may communicate the opposite.
A respectful title must always be accompanied by a respectful tone.
Therapists must never use "Sir," "Ma," "Madam," "Manager," or any title as sarcasm, mockery or a way of undermining the person.

sections.title: 7. Addressing Leaders
paragraphs: Zura Spa recognizes leadership roles because responsibilities must be clear.
Leaders should therefore be addressed appropriately using their recognized leadership role, or their professional work name where appropriate.
Examples: Manager, SM, CM, SP, LT, TG, Therapist Jane / Thr. Jane.
A therapist may be personally close to a leader, but that familiarity should not remove professional respect during work.
I may know this person personally, but while carrying out their work responsibility, I respect the role they represent.

sections.title: 8. Leadership Titles Do Not Make Someone Superior as a Person
paragraphs: Professional respect for leadership does not mean leaders are permitted to insult therapists, shout unnecessarily, humiliate others, belittle junior staff, or speak disrespectfully because of position.
Leadership titles communicate responsibility, not greater human value.
A Manager, SM, CM, SP, LT or TG is expected to demonstrate the same respect they expect from others. The standard works both ways.

sections.title: 9. Addressing Colleagues
paragraphs: Colleagues should communicate professionally even when they are friends.
The normal professional form is Therapist + Work Name, Thr. + Work Name, or recognized leadership title where applicable.
Examples: "Therapist Jane, please can you assist me?" "Thr. Clara, Client Sam is ready." "LT, please can you check this technique?"
Colleagues should not address each other in ways that belittle, mock, humiliate, sexualize, insult, or intentionally provoke.

sections.title: 10. The Therapist's Mindset
paragraphs: The correct mindset is: "I can be comfortable with people without becoming careless with my words."
Familiarity is not permission for disrespect. Being friends with a colleague does not mean workplace communication can become careless.
Correction is not permission for disrespect. If a colleague or leader corrects you, you should not respond with insults or aggression. Likewise, the person giving correction should remain respectful.
Position does not determine dignity. A person deserves respectful communication whether they are a client, a new therapist, an experienced therapist, a TG, an LT, an SP, a CM, an SM, or a Manager.
Respect should remain consistent. Do not speak politely only when someone important is present. Professional communication should be part of your normal conduct.

sections.title: 11. Relevance of This Standard
list: Creates a welcoming client experience.
Strengthens professionalism.
Makes internal communication clearer.
Reduces confusion about who is being discussed.
Reinforces the leadership structure.
Creates appropriate boundaries.
Encourages mutual respect.
Reduces unnecessary familiarity.
Reduces conflicts caused by careless language.
Helps clients observe a disciplined team culture.
Creates consistency across the spa.
Strengthens the Zura Spa identity.

sections.title: 12. What Good Practice Looks Like
paragraphs: When speaking internally: "Client Sam is ready for his session." Not: "That man is ready."
When speaking to the client: "Mr. Sam, are you comfortable?" or "Are you comfortable, Sir?"
When speaking to a therapist: "Therapist Jane, please assist with Room 1."
When speaking to a leader: "SM, please can I clarify something?" or "SP, Client Sam has a concern."
During a handover: "Therapist Clara, this is Client Sam. Client Sam prefers medium pressure and has some tension around his shoulders."
This creates a professional interaction involving everyone.

sections.title: 13. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite of this standard is a workplace where people are addressed carelessly according to mood, familiarity or perceived importance.

sections.title: Referring to Clients Carelessly
paragraphs: Examples: "That guy." "That woman." "The customer." "The fat man." "The short guy." "The Indian." "The white man." "That old woman."
Apart from being unprofessional, these descriptions can easily become offensive.

sections.title: Calling Colleagues Disrespectfully
paragraphs: Using insults, mocking names, humiliating nicknames, shouting someone's name aggressively, or degrading language is inconsistent with the Zura Spa standard.

sections.title: Ignoring Leadership Roles Deliberately
paragraphs: A therapist should not intentionally refuse professional modes of address because "She's my friend" or "We are all therapists." Roles exist because responsibilities differ.

sections.title: Using Titles Sarcastically
paragraphs: Examples such as "Okay o, Manager!" or "Yes Madam Supervisor!" said mockingly are not respectful simply because a title was technically used.

sections.title: Using Familiarity With Clients Carelessly
paragraphs: Repeated clients may become familiar with therapists. This does not mean therapists should automatically begin using pet names, romantic names, sexualized names, or overly familiar language unless there is an appropriate and professionally acceptable context.
The professional relationship remains.

sections.title: 14. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate Disrespectful Modes of Address
paragraphs: The way people address each other gradually determines workplace culture.
If careless communication is tolerated, it can develop into disrespect, mockery, cliques, arguments, resistance to leadership, poor client boundaries, and workplace hostility.
It may appear small initially: "It's only what I called her." But repeated disrespectful language eventually affects how people treat one another.
For this reason, Zura Spa does not regard mode of address as meaningless. It is part of maintaining order, professionalism and dignity.

sections.title: 15. Impact on the Team
paragraphs: Poor modes of address can affect the whole team.

sections.title: It Weakens Respect
paragraphs: If therapists routinely speak carelessly to one another, disrespect gradually becomes normal.

sections.title: It Weakens Leadership
paragraphs: If recognized leadership roles are openly mocked or deliberately disregarded, it becomes harder for leaders to coordinate the team effectively.

sections.title: It Creates Conflict
paragraphs: Many workplace arguments begin not because of what was said but how it was said.

sections.title: It Creates Cliques
paragraphs: Different people may receive different levels of respect depending on friendship, seniority or popularity. That creates division.

sections.title: It Affects New Therapists
paragraphs: New therapists learn culture by observing existing staff. If they see disrespect normalized, they are likely to reproduce it.

sections.title: It Affects Clients
paragraphs: Clients hear how therapists speak to each other. If therapists are shouting names, mocking one another, using disrespectful language, or ignoring leadership, the client may conclude that the business is poorly managed.

sections.title: 16. What Therapists Should Do
list: Use Therapist + work name or Thr. + work name when addressing colleagues professionally.
Use recognized leadership titles where applicable.
Refer to clients internally as Client + name.
Ask clients for their names where appropriate.
Use Mr. or Ms. + name appropriately.
Use Sir, Ma or Madam respectfully where appropriate.
Maintain a respectful tone.
Maintain respectful facial expressions and body language.
Respect leadership roles.
Maintain professional language even with friends.
Correct colleagues privately and respectfully.
Listen before responding.
Remain respectful during disagreement.
Remember that clients may hear staff interactions.
Address everyone with dignity.

sections.title: 17. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Call clients "that man," "that woman," or similar descriptions when their name is known.
Identify clients unnecessarily by physical appearance.
Give clients disrespectful nicknames.
Use pet names inappropriately.
Call colleagues insulting names.
Mock someone's work name.
Deliberately ignore a recognized leadership role.
Use leadership titles sarcastically.
Shout another therapist's name aggressively across the spa.
Speak to colleagues as though they are inferior.
Use familiarity to justify disrespect.
Address leaders carelessly because of personal friendship.
Speak disrespectfully to junior therapists.
Use Sir, Ma or Madam with a mocking or undermining tone.
Correct people by humiliating them publicly where private correction is appropriate.
Respond rudely because someone corrected you.
Allow anger to determine how you address another person.
Use offensive jokes or humiliating language.
Argue disrespectfully with clients.
Speak differently to someone simply because they appear wealthy, influential or important.

sections.title: 18. Correction and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: Forgetting a title occasionally + accepting correction = normal adjustment. Using the wrong work name + correcting it = learning. Speaking carelessly + recognizing and correcting it = growth.

But: Repeated deliberate disrespect = performance concern. Repeated mocking of colleagues or leaders = professional conduct concern. Deliberately humiliating a client, colleague or leader = disciplinary concern. Using degrading, discriminatory or sexually inappropriate modes of address = serious disciplinary concern.
The objective is not to punish harmless mistakes in wording. The objective is to maintain a culture where respect is intentional and consistent.

items.label: Client (direct address)
items.body: Mr. Sam / Ms. Grace / Sir / Ma / Madam

sections.title: 20. The Zura Spa Mode-of-Address Standard
paragraphs: IDENTIFY → ADDRESS → RESPECT → MAINTAIN
Every therapist has a professional identity: Therapist Jane. Thr. Jane.
Every leadership responsibility should be recognized appropriately: Manager. SM. CM. SP. LT. TG.
Every person receiving our service remains a client: Client Sam. Client Grace.
Every client should be personally and respectfully addressed: Mr. Sam. Ms. Grace. Sir. Ma. Madam.
THE WORD MUST MATCH THE TONE. A respectful title spoken disrespectfully is still disrespect.
At Zura Spa, we can be warm without becoming careless, familiar without becoming disrespectful, friendly without becoming inappropriate, and firm without becoming rude.
Respect the client. Respect leadership. Respect your colleagues. Respect the Zura standard.

remember: The word must match the tone. A respectful title spoken disrespectfully is still disrespect.
